title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
summary: Ground an LLM in your own documents by retrieving relevant chunks and feeding them into the prompt as context.
objectives: Explain why RAG reduces hallucinations and keeps answers up to date
Describe the RAG pipeline: chunk, embed, store, retrieve, generate
Turn text into embedding vectors and store them in a vector database
Retrieve the most relevant chunks using cosine similarity
Build a prompt that grounds Claude in the retrieved context
Cite sources and recognise common RAG failure modes

quiz.q: What problem does RAG primarily solve?
options: It makes the model train faster
It grounds answers in external, up-to-date documents the model never memorised
It removes the need for a prompt
quiz.why: RAG retrieves relevant text from your own data and adds it to the prompt, so the model answers from facts instead of guessing from memory.

quiz.q: In the RAG pipeline, what is an embedding?
options: A copy of the user's question
A numeric vector that captures the meaning of a piece of text
quiz.why: An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) where texts with similar meaning sit close together, enabling semantic search.

quiz.q: Which metric is commonly used to measure how similar two embedding vectors are?
quiz.why: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors; values near 1 mean the texts are semantically close.

quiz.q: Why do we split documents into smaller chunks before embedding?
quiz.answer: So each vector captures a focused idea and retrieval returns precise, relevant passages that fit in the prompt, rather than whole documents.
quiz.why: Chunking keeps embeddings meaningful and lets you pass only the relevant pieces into the limited context window.

quiz.q: What should you do in the prompt to reduce the chance the model invents facts not in the retrieved context?
quiz.answer: Instruct it to answer only from the provided context and to say 'I don't know' when the context lacks the answer.
quiz.why: Grounding instructions plus retrieved context keep the model honest and let it admit gaps instead of hallucinating.

quiz.q: True or false: RAG requires retraining or fine-tuning the language model.
quiz.why: False. RAG adds knowledge at inference time through the prompt, so you can update your data without touching the model.

body_markdown:
## Why RAG?

A language model only knows what it learned during training. Ask it about your company handbook, last week's news, or a private PDF and it will either refuse or, worse, **hallucinate** a confident wrong answer.

**Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** fixes this. Instead of retraining the model, we *retrieve* the most relevant pieces of your own text and paste them into the prompt as context. The model then answers from facts you supplied. As a maths graduate this is a familiar idea: an open-book exam beats a closed-book one.

## The RAG pipeline

RAG has two phases. **Indexing** (done once, offline):

1. **Chunk** — split documents into small passages.
2. **Embed** — turn each chunk into a vector (a list of numbers capturing meaning).
3. **Store** — save the vectors in a vector database.

**Querying** (every question):

4. **Embed the question** with the same model.
5. **Retrieve** the chunks whose vectors are closest to the question.
6. **Generate** — give those chunks plus the question to the LLM.

## Embeddings and similarity

An **embedding** maps text to a point in high-dimensional space so that similar meanings sit near each other. We measure closeness with **cosine similarity** — the cosine of the angle between two vectors. A value near 1 means very similar; near 0 means unrelated.

```python
import numpy as np

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    a, b = np.array(a), np.array(b)
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

# Retrieve top-k chunks for a query embedding
def top_k(query_vec, chunk_vecs, k=3):
    scores = [cosine_similarity(query_vec, c) for c in chunk_vecs]
    return sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda i: scores[i], reverse=True)[:k]
```

## Grounding the generation with Claude

Once you have the top chunks, build a prompt that tells the model to answer **only** from that context. Keep your API key in an environment variable, never in code.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

def answer(question, context_chunks):
    context = "\n\n".join(context_chunks)
    prompt = (
        f"Use ONLY the context to answer. If the answer is not there, "
        f"say 'I don't know'.\n\nContext:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
    )
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text
```

## Failure modes and good habits

RAG is powerful but not magic. Watch for: **bad chunking** (passages too big or split mid-idea), **retrieval misses** (the right chunk never surfaces), and **ignored context** (the model answers from memory anyway). Improve results by tuning chunk size, retrieving a few extra chunks, asking the model to **cite** which chunk it used, and instructing it to admit when it doesn't know.

## Your task

Take three short text files, chunk and embed them, store the vectors, and build a tiny question-answering loop that retrieves the top chunks and grounds Claude in them.

slides.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
slides.narration: Welcome to lesson ten. Today we tackle one of the most useful patterns in real-world A I applications: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG. By the end you'll understand how to ground a language model in your own documents so it answers from facts rather than guessing, and you'll see the whole pipeline from chunking to generation.

slides.title: Why RAG?
bullets: Models only know their training data.
Ask about private or recent data and they hallucinate.
RAG retrieves your text and feeds it to the model.
Like an open-book exam instead of closed-book.
slides.narration: A language model only knows what it saw during training. Ask it about your company handbook or last week's news, and it will either refuse or confidently make something up. We call that hallucination. RAG fixes this by retrieving the most relevant pieces of your own text and pasting them into the prompt. As a maths graduate, think of it as an open-book exam: the model answers from facts you supplied.

slides.title: The pipeline: two phases
bullets: Indexing (once): chunk, embed, store.
Querying (each time): embed question, retrieve, generate.
No retraining of the model at all.
Knowledge is added through the prompt.
slides.narration: RAG has two phases. First, indexing, which you do once offline: you split your documents into chunks, turn each chunk into a vector, and store those vectors. Second, querying, which happens for every question: you embed the question, retrieve the closest chunks, and hand them to the model to generate an answer. Crucially, you never retrain the model. The knowledge enters through the prompt.

slides.title: Chunking documents
bullets: Split long documents into small passages.
Each chunk should hold one focused idea.
Too big: vague vectors. Too small: lost context.
Chunks must fit the context window.
slides.narration: Before we embed anything, we split documents into smaller chunks. Why? Because each chunk becomes one vector, and we want that vector to capture a single focused idea. If chunks are too big, the meaning gets blurry. If they're too small, you lose context. Good chunking is the quiet secret behind good retrieval, and it's worth experimenting with.

slides.title: Embeddings
bullets: An embedding is a vector capturing meaning.
Similar texts land close together.
Same model embeds chunks and questions.
This enables semantic search, not keyword search.
slides.narration: An embedding maps a piece of text to a point in a high-dimensional space, in such a way that texts with similar meaning sit close together. This is what lets us search by meaning rather than by exact keywords. The key rule: use the same embedding model for your chunks and for your questions, so they live in the same space and can be compared.

slides.title: Cosine similarity
bullets: Measures the angle between two vectors.
Near 1 means very similar.
Near 0 means unrelated.
We pick the top-k most similar chunks.
slides.narration: To find the closest chunks we use cosine similarity, which measures the angle between two vectors. A value near one means the texts point in nearly the same direction and are very similar; a value near zero means they're unrelated. For each question we score every chunk and keep the top few. This little function is the whole heart of retrieval.

slides.title: Storing vectors
bullets: A vector database holds embeddings.
It finds nearest neighbours fast.
Examples: Pinecone, Chroma, FAISS.
A list works for tiny demos.
slides.narration: Where do all these vectors live? In a vector database. Its job is to take a query vector and quickly find the nearest neighbours among thousands or millions of stored vectors. Popular options include Pinecone, Chroma, and FAISS. For a small learning project, even a plain Python list with our cosine function works fine. Reach for a real database when scale matters.

slides.title: Grounding the answer
bullets: Build a prompt: context plus question.
Tell the model to answer only from context.
Let it say 'I don't know'.
Keep API keys in environment variables.
slides.code:
prompt = (
  "Use ONLY the context. If missing, "
  "say 'I don't know'.

"
  f"Context:
{context}

"
  f"Question: {question}")
slides.narration: Now we generate. We take the retrieved chunks, join them into a context block, and build a prompt that says: answer using only this context, and if it's not there, say I don't know. That last instruction is what keeps the model honest. And remember, your A P I key lives in an environment variable, never hard-coded in your script.

slides.title: Calling Claude
bullets: Pass the grounded prompt to the model.
Read the text from the response.
Same Messages A P I you already know.
Swap models freely for cost or speed.
slides.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
  model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
  max_tokens=1024,
  messages=[{"role": "user",
             "content": prompt}])
print(msg.content[0].text)
slides.narration: Calling the model is the same Messages A P I you've already used. We create a message with our grounded prompt, set a sensible max tokens, and read the text out of the response. Here we use Claude Sonnet for a good balance of cost and quality, but you can swap to Haiku for speed or Opus for the hardest questions without changing anything else.

slides.title: Failure modes
bullets: Bad chunking splits ideas in half.
Retrieval can miss the right passage.
Model may ignore context and guess.
Fix: tune chunks, retrieve more, ask for citations.
slides.narration: RAG is powerful but not magic. The usual failures are: bad chunking that splits an idea down the middle, retrieval that misses the passage you needed, and a model that ignores the context and answers from memory anyway. The fixes are practical: tune your chunk size, retrieve a few extra chunks for safety, and ask the model to cite which chunk it used so you can check its work.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: RAG = retrieve relevant text, then generate.
Chunk, embed, store, retrieve, ground.
Cosine similarity finds the closest chunks.
Task: build a tiny RAG question-answerer.
slides.narration: Let's recap. RAG means retrieving the most relevant text from your own data and feeding it to the model so it answers from facts. The pipeline is chunk, embed, store, retrieve, and ground the generation. Cosine similarity is how we find the closest chunks.
